Rivals are ordered by a score. A higher score means a tougher rival.
Everything counts only on tables where you played with that rival.
The score adds points for each of these numbers:
• %1$d for each "Ahead of you": a table where the rival finished above you.
• %2$d for each "Deal-in": a hand that you discarded and the rival won.
• %3$d for each "Self-draw": a hand that the rival won by self-draw.
• %4$d for each "Third party deal-in": a hand that the rival won on the discard of another player, not yours.
The sum is divided by the shared tables so a rival is not first only because you met often.

This app collects anonymous data about how people use it and about errors. The team uses the data only to find problems and to improve the app.

The app records the following data: • The screens, dialogs and tabs that you open, and for how long. • The actions that you use, such as saving a table. • Errors and crashes, with technical details such as the type of the error.
The app does not record your name, your email address, your EMA number or any text that you enter. The data does not identify you.

The tables of every round are drawn in one go, before the tournament starts. This is how it works:

• The app fills the tables one seat at a time, round after round.
• For each seat it picks, at random, a player who has no table yet in that round.
• If that player has already played against someone at the table, or is on the same team, it tries another one.
• If at some point nobody fits, it starts again from the beginning.
• It tries many shares at once and keeps the first one that works. Heavy computing tries even more at once, so big tournaments are ready sooner.

• Nobody plays against the same person twice in the whole tournament.\n• In a team tournament, two players of the same team never sit at the same table.\n• The order of the seats at each table is also random.

• The tables are really drawn by chance. There are no formulas, fixed tables or pairing systems behind them.
• Nobody’s ranking, level or country counts. All the tables are decided before the first hand is played.
• Every free player has the same chance of each seat, so no patterns repeat from one tournament to the next.
• Each tournament gets its own draw, and nobody can know beforehand how it will turn out.
• Tip: the draw uses player numbers (1, 2, 3…). Put the names on those numbers without looking at the tables first, for example in sign-up order. That way nobody can choose who they play against.
Several shares at the same time The first one that works wins

With many rounds for few players, or with teams, the first way can take a long time. If it does not finish in time, the app moves on by itself to this second way. It keeps the same rules and is just as random.

• It deals every round at random at once, even if there are repeats.
• It counts the repeats: two players who meet more than once, or two of the same team at one table.
• It takes a player from a table with a repeat and swaps them, within the same round, with the player of another table that removes the most repeats.
• It does not undo a swap it has just made, so it does not go round in circles. If a long time passes with no progress, it makes a few random swaps and goes on.
• When no repeat is left, the draw is ready. At the end it shuffles the order of the tables and of the seats.

• The time limit grows with the number of tables and rounds, because a big tournament needs more time even when it is easy.
• The first way gets 15 seconds, plus 0.1 seconds for each table of each round, up to 1 minute. For example, 16 players and 4 rounds: about 17 seconds.
• The second way gets 30 seconds, plus 0.5 seconds for each table of each round, up to 5 minutes.
• If neither one makes it, the app says so and changes nothing. Taking out one round is usually enough.
The first way was taking too long.\nNow the second way is trying, by swaps.

Third case: more rounds than fit without repeats
Each round a player meets 3 new rivals, so the new rivals run out: 16 players, for example, can play 5 rounds without anyone meeting the same rival twice. With more rounds, the app draws in blocks.

• A block has as many rounds as fit without repeats for that number of players. With teams, one round less. • In the first block nobody meets the same rival twice. In the second, nobody meets them a third time, and so on. The last block, even if it is shorter, keeps the same rule. • With 16, 28, 40 or 64 players there is a perfect pattern: in each block every player meets each rival exactly once. The pattern is always the same shape, but who sits where in it is drawn at random, with a new draw for each block. • With other numbers of players, each block is drawn by swaps, like the second way, counting the tables of the blocks before. • With 16, 28, 40 or 64 players the pattern is also used when the first way does not finish in time, instead of the second way, because it is instant.
